newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-YANKEES' IRABU WINS RETURN TO MAJORS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-YANKEES' IRABU WINS RETURN TO MAJORS.

text.p: Japanese pitcher Hideki Irabu made a successful return to the major leagues Wednesday.
After a 90-minute rain delay, Irabu, staked to an early lead, pitched effectively enough to win as the New York Yankees routed the Kansas City Royals 9-3.

"I had a lot to overcome and work on," Irabu said through an interpreter. "The Yankees gave me an opportunity to work on certain technical aspects, and that was the difference. I wasn't prepared enough the first time."
After debuting last month with a win and much fanfare, Irabu was roughed up in three consecutive starts and returned to the minor leagues.
He showed overpowering form at the lower level again and returned to allow three earned runs and six hits in 5 1/3 innings, walking two and striking out five.
Irabu struck out the side in the first inning and was unscored upon for four innings. He yielded a mammoth sixth-inning home run to Chili Davis.
"The team won today and that's all that matters to me," said Irabu.
"I got my fast ball again and threw a live ball. There was rotation on my fast ball and I utilized the right location in the strike zone."

Irabu's debut on July 10 came in front of a sellout crowd at Yankee Stadium. There was not quite the same fanfare Wednesday as a steady rain kept the crowd down to 31,418 and delayed the start of the game.

Irabu was 2-2 with a 7.97 ERA in his four major league starts for New York and was sent down to Columbus on July 28. After an impressive debut against Detroit, Irabu was shelled in his last three starts, giving up 17 runs and 20 hits in 13 2/3 innings.
Irabu had been rocked in his last major-league start on July 26 against Seattle, allowing six runs and four hits, including two home runs, in just two innings.
"He was a lot better today," Yankees manager Joe Torre said. "He was curious to see what he could do. He pitched well after waiting a couple of hours."
"He was much different today," said catcher Joe Girardi. "His velocity was much swifter. Even when Davis hit the home run he made a good pitch. Davis is a real good major league hitter.
Added Girardi: "He was a lot more relaxed, he made a lot of adjustments in two weeks. He'll get nothing but better."
Under the tutelage of pitching coach Billy Connors, Irabu was 1-0 with a 1.20 ERA in two starts at Triple-A Columbus during his demotion, striking out 15 in 15 innings.

"I thought he used his fast ball much more and it had greater velocity than the other time he was here," said Connors. "He went at them aggressively with his fast ball and that's what we wanted. In the past he lost confidence in his fast ball, and stopped using it.
"He has had an awful lot to learn, both on and off the field. Off the field, they rush him and he has to understand what autographs mean to American fans."
At least one opponent was not impressed, however, especially when comparing Irabu to his countryman Hideo Nomo.

"He is overpublicized and overadvertised," Royals shortstop Jay Bell said. "He's your basic right-hander with a straight fastball. He's not even close to Nomo. From the first game against Nomo, he was great. Irabu doesn't respect the game much."
But Davis said: "He threw hard and his ball moves. I hit a good pitch. He should be able to win in the majors when he knows the hitters better."
Irabu was acquired from the San Diego Padres in April after lengthy trade talks and signed a four-year, $12.8 million contract.
The Yankees shipped $3 million, outfielder Ruben Rivera and minor-league pitcher Rafael Medina to San Diego to get Irabu.

The Padres owned Irabu's rights through their working agreement with his Japanese team, the Chiba Lotte Marines. Irabu was adamant in his desire to pitch only for the Yankees and was prepared to sit out the entire season if he was not traded to New York.
He was 12-6 and led the Japanese Pacific League with a 2.40 ERA last season.
